passage: Kunal, you're worried about telling everyone which wedding rituals you'll skip? Let your Dadi Indu tell you about your father. At twenty-five, before his wedding, he came to me with a list. He wanted to keep the pheras and the blessing of the elders. He wanted a shorter haldi, so your mother's side could join too. And he did not want the ceremony where the bride's family hands over gifts, because he said it made them feel smaller. My husband went red. But your father sat beside him and said, 'Papa, I'm keeping what means something. This one hurts people.' He said it softly, holding his hand. Your Dadaji grumbled for a week, then told the whole street it was his idea.

qa.q: Which rituals did Kunal's father want to keep?
qa.a: The pheras and the blessing of the elders.

qa.q: What was Kunal's father feeling when he sat beside his own father to explain?
qa.a: He felt determined but tender and a little anxious, wanting change without hurting his father's feelings.

qa.q: Which choice in the story made the change acceptable to the family?
qa.a: Explaining softly which rites he kept, which he adapted and which he dropped because it hurt people, while holding his father's hand.

qa.q: How did Kunal's Dadaji come to see the changes?
qa.a: He was upset at first and grumbled for a week, but later embraced them, even claiming the idea as his own.

grounding: Shows a young adult who keeps meaningful rites, adapts one and drops one that hurts others, explaining kindly so the elders can hear the change.

passage:
With two weeks left and a budget that barely covered the hall, Parul, twenty-five, sat with a notebook and Irawati Nani. 'The saat phere, yes. Haldi, yes, but at home, not a hotel. The sangeet, just cousins and a speaker.' Then a pause. 'And Ma will do the rituals with me. All of them.'
Nani's face tightened. Ma had been widowed three years; by custom she would stand at the back.
'Nani, I know it's how it was done in your time. I'm not saying you were wrong. But I can't have Ma hiding at my wedding.'
Nani was silent a long time. Then she said, 'Your Nana would have wanted her in front.'
On the day, Ma stood beside Parul, and Nani wiped her eyes.

qa.q: Where would the haldi be held?
What was Irawati Nani feeling when her face tightened?
qa.a: Nani felt uneasy and perhaps hurt, since the change challenged the custom she had lived by.

qa.q: How did Parul make the change easier for Nani to accept?
qa.a: Parul explained kindly, honoured Nani's past without calling it wrong, and gave a clear reason: Ma should not have to hide.

qa.q: How might Ma have felt standing beside Parul on the day?
qa.a: Ma likely felt included and deeply moved, no longer pushed to the back at her child's wedding.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who keeps some wedding rites, simplifies others and sets aside one that excludes a widowed parent, explaining kindly so the elder can accept it.
